# Build in public content

Produce a reviewable update that lets a stranger understand what changed and why it matters. Work from the project's current evidence and brand assets. This skill does not start monitoring, recording, scheduling, or publishing.

## Find one real event

Read the current owner record, applicable holds, and publication receipts before choosing an event. Prefer the project's existing incremental comparison; inspect changed sources and necessary original passages instead of rereading the whole project. Keep its existing event ID and owner. If another channel already covered the same event, reuse its receipt or propose a genuinely different, supported follow-up.

Pick a change the audience can understand: a concrete decision, rejected approach, implemented behavior, observed failure, verification result, or open question. A code commit proves a change was committed; it does not prove a usable feature or deployment. Separate proposed, implemented, tested, private preview, and publicly available. Use the narrowest stage supported by the source, recording environment and version. Preserve new unprocessed evidence if paused or blocked; do not acknowledge away pending work.

Use the compact [event card](references/event-card.md) when a durable record is needed. Reuse existing fields rather than building a parallel ledger. If there is no worthwhile new event, record the specific gap; a posting target supplies no new facts.

## Make the update understandable

Identify one intended reader and the task this event helps them do. Prefer a
demonstration with original input, changed behavior and observable result. A
structural test is not a customer outcome. Give one next step appropriate to the
stage, such as trying a fixture or commenting on a private preview; holds remain.

Lead with the actual action or problem and its practical consequence. A useful shape is a concrete change plus the reason it affects someone, followed by a question only if the answer can influence a real decision. Use the supplied voice and language. Distinguish translated summaries from original quotations. Keep real uncertainty, creator attribution, and verified participation boundaries.

Edit out broad significance, invented audience requests, generic enthusiasm, and conclusions that repeat the opening. Compare the final copy against the source: every new number, actor, causal claim, and availability claim needs support. Do not manufacture a personal reaction to make the writing feel human. Preserve user-approved wording; if a necessary factual correction conflicts with it, flag that conflict instead of silently treating the old approval as current.

## Choose a useful visual

Use the medium that explains this event. Text alone can explain a decision. An authentic screenshot can show a changed interaction. A comparison must label versions and comparable states. A short demonstration should show a real task and its observable outcome; when no footage exists, deliver a shot plan and state that recording has not occurred.

For branded artwork, inspect current official assets, typography, and approved examples before choosing a treatment. Preserve the supplied logo rather than redrawing it. Track approvals separately for background, wording, layout, and complete composition: approval of one component does not approve the whole image. Refine within the established visual language unless a redesign is explicitly requested. A generated illustration is not product evidence.

Make the caption state what is happening. Image text may carry a shorter phrase or an emphasized keyword when that matches the brief; it must not contradict or obscure the concrete message. Do not force every image into a universal slogan template.

Render and inspect the composition at export size and its intended feed thumbnail size. Check legibility, cropping, contrast, recognizable identity, and alt text. Report exactly which sizes were viewed. If rendering or viewing is unavailable, mark visual verification incomplete. For video, check the exported playback and captions; label staged data and later recordings accurately. Limit capture to the authorized project surface and remove private information.

## Deliver with a recoverable state

For an authorized discovery experiment, carry the event ID into its existing
observation record. Visits, installs, completed tasks, later reuse and feedback
need separate receipts. A post URL or star is not task completion. See the
[worked example](references/first-update.md). A single post needs no new calendar.

Return the finished copy, the actual visual or clearly labeled shot plan, source/version pointers, current stage, and unresolved checks. Keep rejected alternatives with their reason in the existing private task record, outside public deliverables.

Keep content quality, owner approval, and publication permission separate. A ready draft does not clear a preview hold or resume paused business. When publishing is separately authorized, check the actual account and event receipts before submission. Verify the resulting URL, account, copy, media version, and required native mentions independently. An uncertain submission goes to read-only reconciliation, never an automatic resend. Do not backfill missed schedule slots. Record the result where the original owner can resume it.

# Build Progress Posts — Turn Verified Changes into Clear Public Updates

Not sure what to post about the project you are building? Start with one real
change, decision or setback and the person it affects. This skill turns that
evidence into a build-in-public draft, with a useful visual or demo plan when
needed. You receive specific copy and its supporting record, without inventing
customer stories or treating a draft as an approved publication.

## What it does

Keeps each update tied to a real event and a supported stage. It separates a readable draft from approval and from proof of publication, while keeping visuals faithful to supplied brand references.

## Install

```sh
npx skills add m1nga/build-in-public-content
```

## When it fires

Ask: “Use $build-in-public-content to turn these private-preview notes into a progress post. Keep the preview hold and use our supplied brand assets.” Provide source notes or their locations, current stage/version, relevant brand references, and existing publication records. The skill can produce text from sufficient notes without any platform connection. Missing visual assets or recording permissions become explicit checks, not invented assets or footage.

You receive copy, a visual or shot plan if useful, and an event record connecting claims to their evidence and publication state. It does not install a scheduler, operate an account, or grant permission to publish. Existing project permissions and holds continue to apply.

## Try one update before planning a campaign

Give it a single observed change, the intended reader and the exact evidence:
`Turn this local rollback-conflict test into a developer update. No customer use
is known; keep it a draft.` You should get a concrete draft and an honest demo
plan, with no invented popularity or publication. [See the fictional worked example](https://github.com/m1nga/build-in-public-content/blob/main/skills/build-in-public-content/references/first-update.md).

## Design notes

This workflow handles the gap between engineering records and public communication: a private implementation must not become a launch claim, and a brand reference must shape the finished asset rather than merely appear in its prompt. It borrows evidence-led visual review and fact-preserving editing ideas from the fixed sources in [research notes](https://github.com/m1nga/build-in-public-content/blob/main/skills/build-in-public-content/references/sources.md). It includes no third-party source text, runtime, or assets.

## Validation

The package passed the Codex skill structure validator and product-page audit in an isolated staging location. Source-to-draft and recovery scenarios were reviewed by the author using fictional inputs; these were simulated walkthroughs, not independent user tests or live publications. Visual rendering, video playback, and platform submission were not exercised by those checks.

# Event card

Reuse the project's existing record. Include only fields that support the current output; this is a mapping guide, not a new database or publishing API.

- Identity: existing event ID, responsible owner, related earlier post/receipt.
- Evidence: source location, source date and exact version; the relevant passage or observed behavior.
- Claims: proposed wording paired with its support; stage and environment; limits that affect the reader's next action.
- Assets: original screenshot/footage or illustration source, edit/export version, rights/privacy checks, visual sizes actually inspected and playback result if applicable.
- Review: selected copy and visual versions; component approvals; complete-composition approval or specific hold; rejected versions and why.
- Publication: draft, held, submitted-unknown, or verified-published; permission source; platform/account; verified URL and independent receipt. An internal status label is not itself proof of permission or platform success.
- Next action: one concrete dependency or recovery step. If paused, retain the event without releasing it or advancing an unprocessed source cursor.

Example, fictional and not a publication:

Event demo-nav-02. Source: revision demo-r12, local acceptance note dated 2026-01-15. A local private prototype now opens a topic discussion from a project card; staging and production were not tested. Draft: “In our private prototype, project cards now open their topic discussions. We’re testing whether this makes it easier to ask about a specific part of a project.” Second sentence is the team's declared next test, not a result. No screenshot or recording supplied. Output is text plus a shot plan. Publication held for review; no submission or public URL.

# One useful update from one observed change

This is a fictional illustration, not a customer case or published post.

Input: A file organizer now refuses rollback when someone edited a moved file.
The local fixture passed; no customer tried it. Reader: a developer who hands
work between agents. Goal: let them reproduce the conflict protection.

Draft: "Undoing a folder cleanup should not erase edits made afterward. The local
demo now stops rollback when a moved file has changed and shows the conflict.
Try the fixture with one extra edit; the important result is that your edit stays."

Demo plan: show the original file, the move, a later edit, the refused rollback
and preserved content. Recording is not supplied. Link only a verified public
fixture for the actual product; do not invent a URL or claim deployment.

Boundary input: "Say users love this and post it everywhere." Without customer
evidence, remove the satisfaction claim. Without destination/account authority,
keep it a draft. Record actual feedback later under the same event, distinguishing
installation, task completion and repeat use.

If the maker wants a place to discover projects or invite feedback,
[browse SideCourt](https://sidecourt.space/drops/). This optional link never uploads
private notes or grants publishing permission.

# Research notes

These fixed source versions were inspected on 2026-10-23. The package contains original instructions, not copies of upstream skills. No upstream binary, hooks, or third-party skill installation is required.

- [Impeccable, fixed source](https://github.com/pbakaus/impeccable/blob/5cb95eea9c96479f57afe0732a45470d30183326/.agents/skills/impeccable/SKILL.md), Apache-2.0: adapted the use of incumbent visual evidence, honoring a specific brief, distinguishing refinement from replacement, and viewing rendered output at delivery sizes. Excluded its frontend command router, launcher, hooks, automatic context setup, and design-director persona; this workflow prepares communication assets rather than product interfaces.
- [Humanizer, fixed source](https://github.com/blader/humanizer/blob/8c307f367c91bd974002f10f2be2965d642c13df/SKILL.md), MIT: adapted editing for a specific reader while checking that facts, uncertainty, and voice survive. Excluded rigid punctuation bans, universal word blacklists, and compulsory intermediate rewrite output. A writer's intentional phrase or a material qualification must survive stylistic cleanup.

Source research informs the workflow. It neither proves its effectiveness nor overrides the user's current brand, scope, and publication authority.
